claims.text: Mary Celeste was found deserted in the Atlantic in December 1872
She was an American brigantine bound from New York to Genoa with a cargo of industrial alcohol
She was sighted by the British brigantine Dei Gratia and brought into Gibraltar
There were ten people aboard: the captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife, their two-year-old daughter and seven crew
The cargo of barrels of spirits was untouched except for one cask which had started
Every document that could have thrown light on the vessel had been removed
The last entry in the ship's log was dated 24 November
The salvage claim went before the Vice-Admiralty court at Gibraltar and the advocate-general was Frederick Solly Flood
Flood suspected the salvors and suspected murder; the examination produced no proof of crime and no one was charged
The ship was released, sold repeatedly, and wrecked on a reef off Haiti in 1885
In January 1884 Arthur Conan Doyle published 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement' in The Cornhill Magazine
The story was fiction, presenting a mutiny aboard the ship, and was widely read as fact
The story spelled the name Marie Celeste, and that spelling passed into common use
The captain was Benjamin Briggs and his wife and their two-year-old daughter were aboard
One small boat was gone from the deck and nothing else had been forced
The vessel had been alone for about ten days before she was found
Flood wrote to his superiors that he suspected crime
The story gave the ship a different name, crew and a villain
Readers wrote to the press asking whether the story was true
Later retellings added details absent from the record
